cells.tense: You're tending the fire right now — feeding it what it needs, and feeling it answer.
cells.ask: Let yourself dream one step past what already works — not to replace the fire, just to see what it would want to burn next.
cells.core: This is a good place to stand. The fire is warm and it's yours — people come to it because of how you keep it, and you keep it without burning your own hands. You've carried this thing through seasons that would have put it out, and you did it by caring for it, not by forcing it. The warmth is real, and it's showing. But staying here isn't the whole of what this is for. The same steadiness that keeps a fire alive is what makes the next imagining safe to try. Dream from what's already been lived, not from what's missing. What you've taken in and made yours is exactly what lets a new picture arrive without wrecking what's here.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the fire going, and you're free to see what it wants to light next.
cells.verb: keeping a fire going — feeding it, guarding it, handing it to others
cells.place: the place where you become what you are — not what you achieved, what you always were

cells.tense: You're bracing two winters ahead — feeding a fire that hasn't been lit yet.
cells.ask: Check one thing being carried before carrying it — and if it isn't here yet, set it down.
cells.core: When this is clean, it's simple: you feel something move in you, and you move with it, tending what's actually in front of you. The fire is lit because there's something real to keep. Right now you're keeping something warm that isn't cold yet. The effort is real; the target keeps moving. You plan the next three ways this could go before you've been given the first one, and the planning feels like tending — except nothing is burning, and your arms are full. The care is all there. What's missing is the honest look at whether what's in front of you is lit, or just the outline of a fire you already decided to tend. Checking isn't distance. It's what keeps the fuel from going to a fire that isn't there.

cells.tense: You stopped months ago — and you're still standing in front of the cold hearth, holding the bellows.
cells.ask: Release one thing already over — and let the letting-go be the first new warmth.
cells.core: There's a fire here worth tending. Going well, this is the part of you that doesn't just feel a direction — it keeps the conditions for it alive, day after day, warmly, without forcing anything. Other people borrow your steadiness; the room stays warm because you're in it. Right now the hearth is cold and the tools are still in your hands. What keeps it that way isn't laziness. Something finished is still taking up your arms, and the load hasn't been put down. Setting it down doesn't repair the ending. It's the one act that makes room for something to start. Nothing has to be lit today except the letting-go.

cells.tense: You're already keeping it going — and the story is that the fire does it by itself.
cells.ask: Name one thing being tended right now — and say out loud that the keeping is yours, before anything else.
cells.core: Going well, this looks like knowing you're the one who keeps the room warm — you arrange, you check, you show up, and you'd say so plainly. That's the capacity doing exactly what it does. Plenty stays lit because of the arranging, the small consistent acts nobody sees, and it's been happening all along. What hasn't happened is the claim. The keeping runs in the background, described as momentum, or as the project moving on its own — so the one person responsible for it never gets credit, and the work feels like something that happens rather than something being made. Naming the tending isn't pride. It's the simple admission that returns the whole thing to your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You're already tending it. You just haven't said that's what you're doing.
